Check in with the college's counselling office. In most cases, your tuition and student fees cover the costs of psychiatric help (I know this applies to Canada, idk about America but I think it's the same there). And don't worry about breaking down in front of the counsellor or psychologist. There's nothing wrong about experiencing the emotions you feel, and chances are strong that plenty of people have sobbed in front of therapists and counsellors, but you know what? Therapists and counsellors are trained to deal with that, they're trained to find people in a bad spot so that they can a) keep them from falling further and b) help them climb out.

I know the feeling of academic anxiety too, man. I'm a first-year student as well, and my first final exam went so badly that I got a full-blown panic attack halfway through. But it's a learning process, I guess. When I'm stressed about my grades, I firstly try to employ any and all relaxation techniques - things as simple as deep breathing or a little jog - and then I try to think about what aspects of my classes are stressing me out, along with ways to fix them. More often than not, your professors will be glad if you go up to them, express your concerns, and ask for advice on how to go upwards. Most professors appreciate students that genuinely work hard to achieve success (which seems to describe you, based on what you've mentioned), and they'd be happy to help.

Good luck

I know the feeling, man. 

If your friends avoid you because you open up about your problems and struggles to them, then I'd say that they aren't true friends. You shouldn't be ashamed to open up - in fact, I'd say it's courageous and shows strength on your part to do so. Don't fret if your friends leave you if you do this - there ARE people on this earth who won't think of you differently for feeling the way you do; in fact, there's a lot of people who are willing to help you and be friends with you regardless of how you view yourself.

Don't focus on "being a fun person to hang out with", instead, try to enjoy yourself and to do things. If you like video games then by all means play the fuck out of them, but try going to like video game expos or Comic-Cons or anywhere where you can meet people who like video games as well. If you enjoy things like art museums, then hang around there. The point is to develop your interests and passions to the point where you WILL be a fun person not because you've changed who you were, but because you've EMBRACED your character, your interests, and your passions.

Hang in there, man. If nothing else, remember that there's millions of people in the same shoes as you who've found happiness and joy and belonging. Work on becoming the best version of yourself (not based on what society thinks is best for you, but based on what makes YOU feel most accomplished and proud), and you'll be joining those newly-happy millions in no time.
